</figure> </div> </div><p>In August, the Alsip village board approved a resolution to place this question on last week’s ballot: “Shall the Village of Alsip modify its current term limits so that no person shall be eligible to seek election to, or hold the office of Village President (Mayor), Village Clerk, or Village Trustee if that person has already served four (4) consecutive four-year terms in that specific office, rather than the current limit of three (3) consecutive four-year terms?”</p><p>The resolution includes other wording similar to Kitching’s long-ago argument, saying “the Mayor and Board of Trustees recognize that maintaining experienced leadership while continuously encouraging qualified public service ensures efficient and stable municipal management.”</p><p>An extra four years in office would provide an obvious benefit for Ryan should he run again and win. He’d not only stay in power longer, he’d continue to get paid by taxpayers and accrue more service credits that would boost his public sector pension.</p><p>Ryan said of the referendum passing: "The voters have spoken definitively. Their mandate establishes this new standard based on the verifiable stability, management and over $500 million in economic development our administration has facilitated here since I was elected in 2017."</p><p>"We will continue focusing on growth that benefits every single resident and local institution in Alsip."</p><p>The recent election saw other local ballot questions on term limits, including in:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-11c99bc2-d9fb-11f1-93df-81046f5e36ad"><li>Calumet Park, where a referendum passed with a 90% yes vote. The measure would make municipal officeholders “subject to new term limits prospectively” that would mean “no person may seek election to, or hold, the same office for more than three (3) consecutive, full, four (4) year terms.”</li><li>Crestwood, where a referendum passed with 91% of voters in favor. The measure would limit elected officials to “no more than three (3) full four-year terms, beginning at the next municipal election.”</li><li>Highland Park, where 75% of voters backed a referendum limiting municipal elected officials to two full four-year terms per office, “whether or not those terms were served consecutively.”</li><li>Markham, where a referendum passed with 92% of voters in favor. The measure would mean no elected official can serve “in the same office for more than two (2) full four-year terms,” starting with the next local election.</li><li>Niles, where a referendum was approved by 68% of voters instituting a 16-year term limit for trustees.</li></ul><p>Other local suburbs already with term limits include Skokie and Tinley Park. Most major U.S. cities except Chicago have term limits for their mayors.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2020/10/2/21496244/alsip-mayor-john-ryan-salary" target="_blank" >To get elected, Alsip Mayor John Ryan bragged of cutting predecessor’s pay. Three years later, he wants a big raise.</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/7/28/23810213/alsip-safespeed-red-light-camera-federal-investigation-subpoenas" target="_blank" >In Alsip red-light camera investigation, feds have done new interviews, issued subpoenas</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/11/1/20943920/michael-madigan-son-andrew-alsip-mayor-john-ryan-campaign-michael-del-galdo" target="_blank" >Speaker Madigan’s son got Alsip business, hit up mayor for campaign cash for his dad</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2019/10/7/20903665/we-dont-pay-people-off-ceo-red-light-camera-company-plays-defense-amid-probe" target="_blank" >‘We don’t pay people off,’ CEO of red-light camera company insists amid federal investigation</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Gunman bursts into Gresham home, sexually assaults woman, police say
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are searching for a man who broke into a Gresham home where he sexually assaulted a woman and robbed her Friday morning on the South Side. </p><p>The 19-year-old woman was home alone in the 7700 block of South Racine Avenue around 10:35 a.m. when the man — believed to be between 40 to 55 years old — forcefully entered, robbed her and sexually assaulted her while he was armed with a handgun, police said. </p><p>He was last seen wearing a blue hoodie, red baseball cap, white medical mask, black pants and red shoes with white laces, police said.</p><p>The Cook County Crime Stoppers are offering a $1,000 reward for any information that leads to an arrest in the case. </p><p><i>"</i>An individual committing this violent and senseless act in someone's home is deeply disturbing. No one should ever have to experience this kind of terror, especially in the safety of their own home," said Paul Rutherford, Executive Director of Cook County Crime Stoppers. "Even the smallest piece of information could make a significant difference in this investigation."</p><p>Anyone with information is encouraged to contact Area 2 detectives at 312-747-8271 or Cook County Crime Stoppers at 1-800-535-7867. </p>

records shows. That leaves the door open for most survivors to come face-to-face with their attackers on campus. Survivors who stay in college often battle mental health challenges and struggle to go to class and focus, according to survey data.</p><p><b>School records</b>: Between 2007 and 2025, the university expelled just seven of 36 students that a disciplinary committee determined had committed sexual assault, according to UChicago reports detailing whether students were found responsible for sexual misconduct and, if so, how they were disciplined. Nineteen sexual assaults were punished with suspension, with some students allowed to return to campus in as little as nine weeks, reports show.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Scrutiny of how universities hold students accountable for sexual violence has intensified following <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydhrlddt-l-u/" target="_blank" >an alleged gang rape at Cornell University</a>. Following <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydhrlddt-l-o/" target="_blank" >two recent reports</a> of sexual assaults with ties to UChicago, students there want <a href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydhrlddt-l-th/" target="_blank" >Cindy Hernandez</a></h5><p>More than 40 years ago, Bernadette McGonagle brought her 4-year-old daughter to the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry to see the Christmas trees and kick off the holiday season. It became an annual tradition, and on Saturday, McGonagle, her daughter and her grandson were there in their best holiday-themed attire for the museum's Tree Lighting and Cultural Festival.</p><p>The tree lighting and festival mark the start of the museum's annual Christmas Around the World and Holidays of Light exhibit.</p><p>The tradition began in 1942 with a single tree decorated to represent a different country each day for 12 days, symbolizing unity among allied nations during World War II, according to Matt Porth, the museum’s deputy director of guest engagement.</p><p>Now the museum displays more than 50 holiday trees decorated to represent countries from around the globe. Each tree is decorated by volunteers who sign up to represent a country.</p><p>"They’re constantly stepping up their game," Porth said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydhrlddt-l-tk/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What marks the beginning of the holiday season in Chicago for you? 🎁</b> </p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: Brief gush of 'much colder air' may usher in first snowflakes of season for Chicago area Friday
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago area could see the "first flakes of the season" though no accumulation is going to happen during a brief cold stretch expected to arrive by Friday morning, weather forecasters say. </p><p>The lows Thursday and Friday are 33 and 30 degrees respectively, which could create conditions for lake effect snowflakes mixed in with rain and thunderstorms but not accumulating snow, according to the National Weather Service. </p><p>"It will be a relatively short-lived period of colder weather there before we warm back up," said Kevin Birk, a meteorologist with the weather service.</p><p>"There is going to be a change here in the weather pattern and it's going to allow for much colder air to spill in across the area here towards the weekend," said Birk. "That could set the stages for some rain, maybe even some potential for some snowflakes."</p><p>Until then, conditions are expected to be cloudy with highs in the 60s Monday and Tuesday and dip into the 50s and 40s Wednesday, according to the weather service. </p><p>Come Sunday, we will return to 50-degree weather, according to the weather service. </p><p>"It will be a relatively short-lived period of colder weather there before we warm back up," Birk said.<br></p>

entries.title: Emma Lozano wins District 7a Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 7a neighborhoods: South Lawndale, Near West Side, Lower West Side, Garfield Ridge, Archer Heights

Longtime Pilsen activist Emma Lozano will continue to represent the majority-Latino District 7a on the Chicago School Board after winning a close race.

As of Monday, Lozano had received nearly 54% of the vote with all precincts reporting, according to the Associated Press.

Election officials have until Nov. 17 to finish counting mail-in ballots and provisional ballots. Final official results are due on Nov. 24.

Lozano, first appointed in 2024 by Mayor Brandon Johnson, faced a challenge from Jesus Ayala Jr., a Chicago Public Schools graduate who worked for a nonprofit after-school program.

Lozano was endorsed by the Chicago Teachers Union, while Ayala had the backing of charter school advocates, groups that oppose the CTU and the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council — which represents thousands of support staff in CPS and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years. Ayala tried to run in 2024, but his name was removed from the ballot after a successful challenge to the signatures on his nomination paperwork.

Ayala had raised $74,000 more than Lozano but she said the decades she spent advocating for education issues gave her the edge in the race.

“I think people remember that and that was able to carry me through,” Lozano said just after 10 p.m. Tuesday.

For Lozano, being part of Tuesday’s election felt like a revolutionary act, recalling a time when community members fought to get an elected school board. She was critical of how much money was poured into the various races.

Lozano will have to work with Jessica Biggs, who won the race for board president and was supported by groups who oppose the Chicago Teachers Union. Lozano said she would respect the election results but she won’t budge on her principles when it comes time to vote on matters before the board.

“There’s going to be some times, hopefully not just myself but others, will have to keep [Biggs] in her place,” Lozano said, adding that she wants to ensure resources are allocated to students living in mixed-status immigrant homes and providing better school lunches.

This Southwest Side district is home to 48 public schools. Last year, 64% received the state’s second-highest designation, “commendable,” while 4.5% received an “intensive” designation, indicating they remained among the bottom 5% of low-income schools in the state for four years after receiving comprehensive support or continued to have a graduation rate of 67% or below.

The students who attend District 7a schools are primarily Latino, matching the community demographics, and most come from families with low incomes. Nearly half are English learners.

Both Lozano and Ayala identified protecting immigrant communities and securing progressive revenue among their priorities.

entries.title: La Ciudad de Chicago niega el permiso de General Iron y es sostenido por una corte del estado
entries.summary: <p>La decisión de la Ciudad de negar el permiso de operaciones a una empresa trituradora de metal del lado sureste por preocupaciones sobre la contaminación del aire y la salud pública fue confirmada por una Corte de Apelaciones estatal el viernes.</p><p>La operación de chatarra, General Iron, reubicada y cambiada de nombre, ya estaba construida y lista para abrir en East 116th Street junto al Río Calumet cuando la administración de la entonces alcaldesa Lori Lightfoot rechazó el permiso, citando el posible impacto en la salud pública por la contaminación del aire.</p><p>La empresa recoge autos desechados, electrodomésticos grandes y otras fuentes para recuperar metal y revenderlo.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c00000" name="module-c00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El propietario del negocio argumentó que la Ciudad no siguió sus propias reglas al tomar la decisión de negar el permiso. Al propietario, conocido como General III, se le permitió construir su instalación porque recibió un permiso de construcción del estado.</p><p>General Iron operó en el vecindario de Lincoln Park durante décadas, incluso cuando la comunidad a su alrededor se gentrificó. Promotores inmobiliarios, funcionarios de la ciudad y vecinos que veían el negocio como una molestia presionaron para que el negocio se mudara.</p><p>Cuando se anunció que la empresa se mudaría al vecindario de East Side, mayoritariamente latino, se desató un rechazo en todo el lado sureste. Defensores comunitarios, de la salud y ambientales se movilizaron y presionaron a Lightfoot para que negara el permiso.</p><p>Una investigación federal por derechos civiles determinó que trasladar el negocio desde una comunidad blanca anglosajona hacia un vecindario latino rodeado por comunidades predominantemente negras fue discriminatorio.</p><p>Reserve Management Group, el propietario mayoritario de General III, ha sostenido que la Ciudad añadió una evaluación de impacto en la salud tarde en el proceso de decisión y que esto excedía el alcance de la revisión de la solicitud. Luego solicitó a un juez administrativo de la Ciudad que considerara si la empresa había cumplido los requisitos para obtener el permiso.</p><p>Ese juez falló a favor de General III, lo que llevó a la administración del alcalde Brandon Johnson a impugnar esa decisión ante la corte de circuito.</p><p>En agosto de 2024, la corte de circuito dictaminó que la Ciudad actuó dentro de su derecho al negar el permiso. La empresa apeló entonces esa decisión ante la Corte de Apelaciones del Primer Distrito de Illinois, integrada por tres jueces, que ahora ha confirmado nuevamente la denegación del permiso.</p><p>En un comunicado, la empresa, que iba a cambiar su nombre a Southside Recycling, dijo que llevará su caso a la Corte Suprema de Illinois.</p><p>"Nuestra instalación ecológica y de última generación cumple con todas las normas ambientales y de salud pública aplicables a nivel municipal, estatal y federal", decía el comunicado. "Seguimos plenamente comprometidos con obtener el permiso de operaciones".</p><p>La Ciudad también ha argumentado que el negocio de metales estaría ubicado en una área de la ciudad que ya sufre una cantidad desproporcionada de contaminación.</p><p>"La Corte reconoció acertadamente que la decisión estuvo bien fundamentada en datos sustantivos y en un análisis detallado de los riesgos que la instalación propuesta tendría sobre la salud pública, la seguridad y el medio ambiente", dijo la Ciudad en un comunicado tras la sentencia.</p><p>Cheryl Johnson, cuya organización fue una de las tres que presentó una denuncia que dio lugar a la investigación federal por derechos civiles, elogió la decisión de la corte.</p><p>"Nos merecemos tener aire, agua y suelo limpios al igual que cualquier otra parte de la ciudad", dijo Johnson, directora ejecutiva de People for Community Recovery (PCR) "Vamos a seguir luchando por eso".</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Michilla 'Kyla' Blaise wins West Side District 5b Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 5b neighborhoods: North Lawndale, Near West Side, East Garfield Park, West Garfield Park, West Town 

Michilla “Kyla” Blaise will continue to represent a large swath of the West Side on the Chicago School Board after winning a close race for District 5b.

Blaise, a political aide backed by the Chicago Teachers Union, received just over 52% of the vote, with all precincts reporting Monday, according to the Associated Press. Election officials have until Nov. 17 to finish counting mail-in ballots and provisional ballots. Final official results are due on Nov. 24.

Blaise, who was appointed to the school board in 2024 by Mayor Brandon Johnson, beat out challenger Anthony Hargrove, who made a second attempt at the seat after failing to make the ballot two years ago.

Hargrove, who runs programs to help dropouts get back in school, had support from the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents CPS support staff, charter school advocates like the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and the Common Ground Collective, an anti-CTU political action committee that’s heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks.

District 5b is one of the school board’s most economically diverse, stretching from the wealthy West Loop to historically disinvested neighborhoods such as North Lawndale and Garfield Park. It includes several neighborhood high schools struggling with declining enrollment, as well as some of CPS’ most in-demand magnet schools. Students who attend school here are mostly Black and Hispanic.

Students in District 5b are less likely to attend their neighborhood school than students in any other voting district in the city. Only 6% chose their local high school, while 35% chose their neighborhood elementary school.

The candidates homed in on different issues during the race. Blaise said she was focused on increasing funding for CPS, addressing declining enrollment and improving student mental health, while Hargrove zeroed in on improving reading and math proficiency, refining special education and expanding vocational and career education.

The two candidates aligned on some issues. They both support stronger restrictions on the use of artificial intelligence and cellphones in the classroom, and both oppose closing schools for any reason.

Notably, Blaise led the effort to pass a CPS budget that reversed some proposed cuts but banked on the state to provide $150 million in funding it had not committed. On his candidate questionnaire, Hargrove said the school board should continue to advocate for additional state funding and look for other savings “before cutting classroom programs or student services.”

Contributing: Mary Norkol

entries.title: Chicago man accused in fatal shooting of violence interrupter Andre Thomas in Chicago Heights
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago man is behind bars Monday facing murder charges in the death of violence interrupter Andre Thomas who was gunned down at his Chicago Heights office on Halloween.</p><p>Alex D. Morris, 54 and of Chicago, has been charged with first-degree murder and was expected to appear for a detention hearing Tuesday at the Markham Courthouse, Chicago Heights police said in a statement. </p><p>Morris was arrested Friday without incident in the area of 95th Street and Perry Avenue in Chicago, according to the statement. </p><p>The first week of investigations yielded the identification of multiple persons of interest, including Morris, according to the statement. </p><p>Information regarding those additional persons of interest as well as specifics of the investigation will not be released at this time as the investigation is ongoing, according to the statement from police. </p><p>Thomas, the Integrity & Fidelity CEO who dedicated his life to reducing gun violence and building safer communities, was celebrated by those who loved and worked with him during a balloon release honoring him last week. </p><p>Thomas was found about 9:25 p.m. Oct. 31in his Chicago Heights office in the 400 block of West 14th Street, Chicago Heights police and the Cook County medical examiner’s office said. Thomas, of Matteson, had suffered multiple gunshot wounds, according to the medical examiner’s office, which ruled his death a homicide.</p><p>Thomas founded I&F in 2021 to educate communities in the south suburbs and Chicago about alternative conflict resolution strategies, intervene in street conflicts by building relationships and responding in real time, and to connect residents with support services, according to the organization’s website.<br></p>

entries.title: Rupert Cintron, a 51-year-old Chicago truck driver, makes his unlikely pro sumo wrestling debut
entries.summary: <p>If ever there was an underdog Chicago could get behind, Rupert Cintron is it.</p><p>Cintron, a 51-year-old Chicago-area truck driver, made his debut as a pro sumo wrestler in a new league that swung through Chicago over the weekend.</p><p>"It's just an opportunity at my age to be able to do something like this," Cintron told the Sun-Times before his first pro match. "I'm 51 years old, and I'm about to get out there with these kids, and, you know, it's just cool ... It's like life never ends if you don't let the dream end. Just keep going."</p><p>With little sumo experience to his name, Cintron is very much just a dude in the right place and time who was given a shot.</p><p>He hasn't worked out — in a gym, at least — in seven years.</p><p>But he moves about 11,000 pounds of flour, beef and other raw materials on a daily basis from his truck into the basements of Chicago restaurants. Before that he worked as a mover.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f70000" level and put on a show, it was awesome," Cintron said Sunday morning on his way to sumo practice.</p><p>"I'm OK, I've just got the regular aches and pains of a 51 year old," he said.</p><p><b>Sumo in Chicago </b></p><p>The majority of wrestlers for the new pro league were pulled from the ranks of the 50 or so amateur sumo clubs around the country that are home to several hundred wrestlers with a wide variety of backgrounds. </p><p>The current amateur sumo scene in Chicago can largely be traced back to Matt Shields, a project manager for a west suburban architecture firm who started the Chicago Sumo Club in 2022 through sheer force of will.</p><p>Shields, 40 and wiry thin, caught the sumo bug while visiting Japan and decided to do something about it upon returning to Chicago.</p><p>In search of members, he brought a thick braided rope to the beach in Humboldt Park to form his sumo ring and began drilling alone, hoping to persuade curious passersby to join him. No one joined. </p><p>Undeterred, he tried a few other spots.</p><p>Shirtless, and wearing compression shorts under his sumo belt, known as a mawashi, he walked up to people enjoying barbecues at 31st Street Beach and asked if anyone wanted to wrestle him.</p><p>"It was mostly African American gentlemen, and they kind of gave me the side eye, like 'Who is this white guy?'" recalled Shields.</p><p>Again, no one took him up on the offer.</p><p>"I understand their reluctance," said Shields in retrospect.</p><p>He used the same tactic at a picnic held by the Japanese American Service Committee of Chicago, where his earnestness drew several participants.</p><p>He eventually formed a group with about 12 core members, including female wrestlers.</p><p>They practice every Sunday at space provided by a local university. They glean instruction from YouTube and the occasional help Ryuichi Yamamoto, a retired Japanese pro sumo wrestler who lives in St. Louis.</p><p>Cintron is a mainstay of the club. So was Rodriguez until he left to help start a separate group, Illinois Sumo Association.</p><h3>Small but growing sport</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Bulls' Caleb Wilson still alive and well in Rookie of the Year running
entries.summary: <p>There will be a time and place for Caleb Wilson to assess the competition.</p><p>That’s when the Bulls rookie can decide if he will attempt to play assassin or take a more passive approach and let the ball bounce where it may.</p><p>Don’t bet on the latter.</p><p>“Nah, I feel like that’s on them whatever they do,” Wilson said recently when asked if he was keeping tabs on his fellow rookie class. “I get my chance to play everyone, and I’ll focus on that chance when I get it. Honestly, I feel like I’m learning so much and going through so many things, I can’t worry about anyone else. I feel like I’ve got to focus on myself.”</p><p>Check back in about a week.</p><p>While the start of the 2026-27 regular-season campaign was a gauntlet of playoff-to-championship level teams to try and navigate, Wilson gets to reunite with some of the key figures in the June draft class, starting on Friday when Atlanta comes to town.</p><p>No. 8 overall pick Kingston Flemings isn’t the reason the Hawks are in the top half of the Eastern Conference through the first furlong of the season, but he has started the last three games with veteran CJ McCollum volunteering to move to the bench, allowing Kingston to have some moments.</p><p>Wilson will see Cleveland’s sneaky second-round pick Meleek Thomas (12.3 points per game) twice in the next few weeks, Brooklyn’s Mikel Brown Jr. (No. 6 pick overall) next week, and the big one on Nov. 20 when the Bulls host Washington and No. 1 overall pick AJ Dybantsa.</p><p>The BYU product was slowed at the start of the season with an ankle issue but has been up and running for the Wizards, flashing some of the skills that made him a first-team All-American as a true freshman.</p><p>According to the latest Vegas odds, Wilson now sits fifth in the Rookie of the Year campaign, led by Memphis’ Cameron Boozer (No. 3 overall pick), Golden State’s Yaxel Lendeborg (No. 11), Sacramento’s Darius Acuff Jr. (No. 7), Dybantsa and then Wilson.</p><p>No. 2 selection Darryn Peterson is right behind Wilson but is making a push with back-to-back 20-point games, including a 26-point performance Sunday against the Timberwolves.</p><p>The one lock to throw money at? That this rookie class has been as good as advertised and is already making an impact around the Association.</p><p>Does that mean Wilson will find his chase for Rookie of the Year too difficult of a race to run? Not really when it goes under a microscope:</p><p></p><p>Boozer – Contender – The Duke product has the highest floor of the entire class just because of his skillset and the opportunity to showcase it. As expected, he’s averaging a double-double, but he’s also handed out 5.2 assists per game and already has a triple-double on the resume.</p><p></p><p>Acuff Jr. – Pretender – There’s no doubt he can score but the guard obviously has the green light as soon as the car pulls in the arena parking lot. He’s fourth in the NBA with 23 shots a game and doing it on an awful team.</p><p></p><p>Peterson – Contender – Injuries have handcuffed Utah somewhat and Peterson is in perfect position to fill a void for a team that has some talent.</p><p></p><p>Lendeborg – Contender – Captured the early-season hype with his trash-talk session with Luka Doncic and has two 30-plus point games. The Warriors are still without Jimmy Butler, but Lendeborg’s moxie has staying power.</p><p></p><p>Dybantsa – Pretender – He could very well be the best player in the class in a few years but is a fourth option behind shot-heavy Trae Young and Anthony Davis. Throw Kyshawn George in the mix and Dybantsa has to wait in line on too many nights.</p>
entries.author: Joe Cowley

entries.title: Bucs QB Baker Mayfield accuses Bears of mimicking his cadence
entries.summary: <p>The Buccaneers had five false start penalties <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Sunday night</a>.</p><p>Quarterback Baker Mayfield didn’t think it was because of the crowd noise.</p><p>The final false start, he claimed, was a result of Bears defenders mimicking his own cadence, which would be illegal. Down eight halfway through the fourth quarter, tackle Tristan Wirfs was whistled on second-and-three.</p><p>“The last one, I know they're barking out the cadence, which, you can't do that,” he said Sunday night after the Bears' 27-24 win. “Tough for the refs to call that because they’re not right there at the line of scrimmage. But yeah, I think they called that on Tristan, but you can’t do that.”</p><p>Bucs coach Todd Bowles said his team was able to hear itself well inside Soldier Field.</p><p>“It wasn’t a communication thing,” he said. “We’ve just got to hold up more.”</p><p>The Bears have benefited from 23 pre-snap penalties by opposing offenses this year, per NFLPenalties.com, which is the fourth-most in the league.</p>

entries.title: College Football Playoff expands to 24 teams, eliminating league title games
entries.summary: <p>The College Football Playoff will double in size to 24 teams beginning next year, bringing an end to a three-decade era of conference title games that used to be among the marquee events of the season.</p><p>College leaders announced the new format Monday, after ESPN agreed to rework its contract to add the 11 new games. Terms were not announced, though ESPN said it was a deal for five years and additional $1.7 billion, on top of the $7.8 billion contract that runs through the 2031 season.</p><p>The revenue generated from the new games will presumably make up for the estimated $345 million the Power Four conference title games were worth. ESPN would then not be on the hook for $140 million of the extra money due to cancellation of the title games, the network reported.</p><p>The new format will have five automatic qualifiers — the champions of the Power Four leagues and the best-ranked team in the smaller Group of Six conferences — with the other 19 teams being chosen by a selection panel. Notre Dame does not receive any guarantees, the way it does this year if it's ranked in the top 12 for what will be the last year of the 12-team postseason.</p><p>The top eight seeds will receive first-round byes in the new format and the playoff will start on the second weekend in December, with the first two rounds of games on campus. The traditional Army-Navy game will be played on the first weekend in December, which used to be reserved for conference title games.</p><p>Both the Southeastern and Big Ten conferences, whose approval was needed to adopt this change, and their Power Four brethren — the Big 12 and Atlantic Coast Conference — are banking that most of the additional spots will go to their members so some of the second-tier teams have new motivation to keep spending big in an era of NIL and $50 million football rosters.</p><p>"Opening the playoff to more programs, more student-athletes and more fan bases across the country is great for college football," said Mississippi State president Mark Keenum, who is chair of the CFP board. "We look forward to seeing this expanded format come to life next season."</p><p>The first final for the 24-team playoff remains set for Jan. 24, 2028, in New Orleans. Traditional bowl games will still host the quarterfinal and semifinal rounds.</p><p>As part of the expansion, the CFP is requiring Power Four teams to play at least 10 "qualifying" regular-season games against conference foes, other Power Four opponents and Notre Dame. Group of Six teams will have to play 10 games against conference opponents and a mix of G6 teams, Notre Dame and other independents.</p><p>The agreement guarantees two off weeks during a regular season that will begin the week before Labor Day.</p><p>An NFL-sized playoff changes the nature of the college regular season</p><p>The move to 24 teams marks the second expansion of the playoff since it began in 2014 as a modest four-team affair. Right after it moved to 12 in 2024, most thought it would eventually max out at 16, which was the SEC's preference.</p><p>But the Big Ten wanted to go bigger, while the SEC balked at that, concerned about the league title game — a property it invented in 1992 and made billions from over the decades — along with the marketability of games featuring third- and fourth-place finishers in power conferences.</p><p>ESPN took care of the money problem. Now, the question is whether fans will embrace an NFL-style free-for-all that could include about one-third of the Power Four's 68 teams, depending on what happens with the Group of Six schools, whose role in these big-money power grabs seems to diminish with every move.</p><p>It's the latest seismic change for a sport that, for decades, built its distinct character and generated controversy by leaning on media and coaching polls to hand out national titles.</p><p>The new system won't be a completely clean break. Critics see a risk in giving more power to a selection committee that hasn't really mastered the four- or 12-team brackets. The exclusion of Florida State in 2023 and Notre Dame last season stand out as the best examples — and the first rankings release of this season left people scratching their heads again.</p><p>Skeptics also view the expanded playoff as another watering-down of what's largely seen as one of the most important regular seasons in sports, replacing potential matchups between, say, Alabama and Georgia in an SEC title game with a 13 seed vs. 20 seed game that would pit, say, Kentucky and South Carolina.</p><p>But, as Big Ten commissioner Tony Petitti argued from the beginning, a postseason that gives bubble teams hope and keeps others vying for home-field advantage or byes will bring more eyes — not fewer — to the end of a regular season that sometimes boils down to only three or four traditional rivalry games with meaning. (One of those traditional games, Ohio State-Michigan, is shaping up to have zero impact on this year's playoffs this year.)</p><p>More at-large berths also help the conferences cash in on the decision to expand their league schedules (the SEC didn't really want to) and demand more non-league games be played among Power Four teams — all in an effort to beef up strength-of-schedule ratings that will carry weight with a selection committee.<br></p>

entries.title: Demanda por derechos civiles denuncia condiciones ‘inhumanas’ en centro de detención de Indiana
entries.summary: <p>Una coalición de organizaciones de derechos civiles —incluidos la ACLU, el National Immigrant Justice Center y el MacArthur Justice Center— presentó una demanda colectiva que impugna el trato "inhumano y constitucionalmente punitivo" a detenidos en una prisión de máxima seguridad de Indiana donde muchos inmigrantes del área de Chicago terminan tras su arresto.</p><p>Una extensa prisión masculina en Bunker Hill, la Miami Correctional Facility, a unas 150 millas de Chicago, abrió alrededor de 2001 y hoy funciona a la vez para presos estatales ordinarios y para inmigrantes detenidos.</p><p>Apodada informalmente "Speedway Slammer" por funcionarios federales, forma parte de una red de más de 250 centros de detención de inmigración en todo el país y se ha convertido cada vez más en una vía regional para quienes son capturados por agentes federales bajo las agresivas políticas de deportación del presidente Donald Trump.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b40000" name="module-b40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los abogados de derechos civiles dicen que las condiciones en la instalación se han vuelto extremadamente peligrosas, lo que ha resultado en violaciones directas de los derechos constitucionales de los inmigrantes detenidos. Desde 2025, al menos dos inmigrantes han muerto mientras estaban bajo custodia. Señalan que la demanda busca responsabilidad y la reversión inmediata de estas duras condiciones.</p><p>"La gente está sufriendo, ha muerto gente, y más gente sufrirá y morirá si eso continúa", dijo Kathleen Hickey, abogada del personal de la ACLU de Illinois que presentó la demanda. "Por eso presentamos esta demanda".</p><p>Las autoridades de Indiana no devolvieron de inmediato las solicitudes de comentarios sobre la demanda. En un comunicado, el Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) negó las acusaciones de las condiciones, argumentando que cualquier afirmación de que los reclusos fueron "maltratados, desnutridos y no recibieron atención médica adecuada" es falsa.</p><p>Entre las demandantes que figuran en la demanda presentada en la Corte de Distrito de los Estados Unidos para el Distrito Norte de Indiana, División de South Bend, está Cynthia Acevedo, una inmigrante transgénero de Guatemala que, según informes, ha pasado meses sin medicación consistente para la epilepsia, lo que le ha provocado múltiples convulsiones graves por semanas que le han causado lesiones físicas, incluidos dientes rotos.</p><p>La demanda alega además que Acevedo fue víctima de una agresión sexual por parte de otro detenido tras su llegada a la Miami Correctional Facility.</p><p>"Los demandados no tomaron su denuncia sobre la agresión durante varios días (a pesar de sus intentos inmediatos por denunciarla), no la examinaron ni le realizaron un kit de violación, no le proporcionaron medicación para prevenir la transmisión del VIH, y no le hicieron las pruebas de VIH solicitadas ni le entregaron resultados de ninguna prueba", indica la demanda.</p><p>Hickey afirma que a otros inmigrantes se les ha negado medicación crítica contra el VIH durante meses. Ella y otros defensores sostienen que las personas detenidas también están atrapadas en un sistema con atención médica y de salud mental peligrosamente inadecuada, agravada por condiciones de vida insalubres y falta de alimento adecuado.</p><p>"Hay un nivel de castigos abusivos y arbitrarios, como el confinamiento solitario, bloqueos excesivos, agentes que usan insultos raciales y antiinmigrantes y un uso excesivo de la fuerza", dijo Hickey.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" el espacio de detención de ICE” en el Centro Correccional Miami, en Bunker Hill, Indiana, incluyendo aumentar la capacidad por 1,000 camas. También dice que el acuerdo fue posible gracias a fondos de la Ley “One Big Beautiful Bill” de Trump.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Santiago Covarrubias/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>En un comunicado emitido el año pasado, DHS anunció que se asociaba con Indiana para "ampliar el espacio de detención de ICE" en la instalación de Miami, incluidas 1,000 camas adicionales. También indicó que el acuerdo fue posible gracias a fondos de la "One Big Beautiful Bill" (Ley Grande y Hermosa) de Trump.</p><p>Los abogados de derechos civiles dicen que también deben responsabilizarse los funcionarios locales de Indiana.</p><p>"El estado de Indiana y el gobierno federal están trabajando juntos para crear un desastre de derechos humanos en una de las cárceles más peligrosas de Indiana", dijo Alexa Van Brunt, directora de la Oficina de Illinois del MacArthur Justice Center. "Las condiciones son crueles y han resultado en la muerte de personas inocentes. Tanto el estado como el gobierno federal deben rendir cuentas por su trato atroz a las personas encerradas en Miami".</p><p>Las denuncias de maltrato en la Miami Correctional Facility no son nuevas. Los abogados de esta demanda también señalan una batalla legal previa en la que la ACLU de Indiana obtuvo recientemente 1.2 millones de dólares en acuerdos por el abuso de reclusos en la instalación.</p><p>Esa litigación se remonta a 2021, provocada por una demanda presentada en nombre del recluso Jeremy Blanchard. Ese caso inicial motivó que decenas de otros presos se presentaran, lo que finalmente derivó en 30 demandas más contra el Departamento de Correcciones de Indiana por lo que los demandantes describieron como condiciones brutales dentro de las "celdas oscuras" de la prisión.</p><p><i>Adriana Cardona-Maguigad cubre inmigración para WBEZ. entries.title: Breaking down White Sox' offseason needs as GM meetings open in Las Vegas
entries.summary: <p>LAS VEGAS – In three weeks, player movement will halt as team owners lock out the players, and talk of the market price of a No. 3 starting pitcher will be replaced with the stupefying details of collective bargaining agreement negotiations.</p><p>Few major deals go down in November in this league, but if past history is indication, it will be easier than trying to finalize the roster while a hastily-arranged spring training is underway. The 2022 White Sox signed three free-agents within the first two days of the last lockout ending, and traded for AJ Pollock two weeks later. All of them contributed less wins above replacement to that year’s team than Elvis Andrus, who signed in mid-August.</p><p>So yes, it would be good if the White Sox checked some items off their to-do list before 11pm on Dec. 1, when the current CBA expires. Could we get a second look at that list?</p><h3>Starting pitching</h3><p>It will be useful next season to track how many innings White Sox starters are actually throwing, accounting for opener usage in a way current statistics cannot. Nevertheless, Sox starters threw the fewest innings in MLB in 2026.</p><p>They don’t talk like they’re secretly getting more than numbers let on.</p><p>“We're going to need more out of our starting pitching,” general manager Chris Getz said last month. “That doesn't mean that Sean Burke, or Noah Schultz or Davis Martin or Luis Castillo or David Sandlin [aren’t] going to be big parts of getting starter innings for us, but there's going to be opportunities to add.”</p><p>Even with Castillo’s $22.75 million salary in tow, Cot’s Contracts estimates the Sox with less than $100 million committed to next year’s payroll. There would be significant room to add even if the team set a cap at $128 million, which was their reported opening day total…in <i>2011</i>. Getz assured the club has “payroll flexibility” to wield. Even if Tarik Skubal is a bridge too far, there are bulk innings to be had in free agency.</p><p>Michael King was 10th in MLB in innings, Kaima Tara is the most intriguing arm in a Japanese market the Sox now scout devotedly, Michael Soroka looked like the starter the club envisioned two years ago. All of them and more are on the market, where the team’s biggest investment of the winter should go.</p><h3>Outfield</h3><p>With promising rookies Sam Antonacci and Braden Montgomery dominating corner outfield reps in the second half, it might surprise that Getz wants an outfielder, even with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/22/the-white-sox-have-openings-in-the-outfield-and-slugging-prospect-caleb-bonemer-is-preparing-to-fill-one" target="_blank" ><u>slugging prospect Caleb Bonemer nearing the majors</u></a>, and Brooks Baldwin and Tanner Murray on the mend.</p><p>But Tristan Peters played in the All-Star Game two weeks before–and Everson Pereira whacked a double and a homer one <i>day</i> before–the Sox traded for fleet-footed Brenton Doyle. Their drive to bolster their outfield defense can’t be underestimated.</p><p>Antonacci energized the lineup, but understandably was a below-average defender in left; a position he first began learning in spring. Montgomery is a potential long-term fixture, but the coaching staff wants significant offseason progress in his ability to elevate the ball.</p><p>Most immediately, Randal Grichuk and Tommy Pham are free agents. With Andrew Benintendi a designated hitter exclusively, a right-handed outfielder who can play scratch or better defense in a corner would tie together a mix heavy on useful pieces, and light on true everyday regulars.</p><h3>Relief pitching</h3><p>Literally every MLB team needs to add relievers every offseason. If and when the White Sox move Grant Taylor and Hagen Smith to starting, they will need to replace the high-leverage options they trusted most this postseason.</p><p>That aside, they simply need to replace the innings shouldered by outgoing free agent Sean Newcomb, who has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/31/white-sox-sean-newcomb-starter-or-reliever-bullpen-will-venable-grant-taylor-sean-burke-free-agency-chris-getz-rotation-relief" target="_blank" ><u>96 ⅓ more reasons to pursue a starting opportunity</u></a> than he already had when the left-hander arrived in Chicago. Coming off Tommy John surgery, Mike Vasil can’t be expected to shoulder all of it.</p><p>Another left-hander would be a good idea. He was better than it looks, but Bryan Hudson had a 6.15 ERA in the second half. Chris Murphy has good stuff, but inconsistent results kept him off the playoff roster. Internally, there are far more right-handed relief options than southpaws.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Morgan Park fires football coach Chris James
entries.summary: <p>Morgan Park fired football coach Chris James on Monday. According to James, a Morgan Park alum widely regarded as the Public League's best coach, he was fired after refusing to immediately decide whether to return next season.</p><p>"I wanted to finish this season before making any decisions," James told the Sun-Times. "I have not taken any job or had any formal interviews with anyone. So I hadn't given them an answer yet. We had two meetings to talk about it. Even if I was going to leave at the end of the season, with everything I have done for Morgan Park, haven't I earned the right to finish the season and go out with my kids?</p><p>"They didn't want to wait for me to make a decision, so they fired me. That's the truth."</p><p>James planned to coach the team on Friday in the Public League playoffs, a consolation tournament. The Mustangs <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/11/07/providence-flashes-a-multidimensional-offense-in-5a-win-against-morgan-park" >lost a close game to Providence</a> in the Class 5A state playoffs on Saturday.</p><p>"I wanted to be at Morgan Park for 30 years," James said. "The principal at Morgan Park didn’t want me to be there."</p><p>According to James, Morgan Park pulled out of the Public League playoffs after firing him.</p><p>"The administration made an announcement and canceled practice and told me at 3 p.m. that I was relieved of my duties as head coach and to turn in my keys," James said. "That's what happened."</p><p>James coached the Mustangs to this season's de facto city championship, winning the Red title by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/17/morgan-park-football-city-championship-kenwood-cps" >knocking off Kenwood.</a> </p><p>Morgan Park was 55-24 in James' nine years as coach with six consecutive state playoff appearances. James has sent nearly 30 players off to college football; his program has produced more high-level college recruits than any other Public League program over the past five years. The Mustangs were the only Public League team ranked in the Super 25 this season.</p><p>James graduated from Morgan Park in 2006 and went on to play college football at Illinois. </p><p>Morgan Park principal Dan Kuzma and CPS did not immediately respond to requests for comment.<br></p>
entries.author: Michael O'Brien

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams must use 4-interception game vs. Buccaneers to to keep growing
entries.summary: <p>With quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/06/bears-qb-caleb-williams-refining-his-potential-by-embracing-simplicity-delivering-efficiency" >Caleb Williams</a> back on the field the past month, it’s been clear <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> go as he goes.</p><p>When he’s sharp, as he mostly has been, the offense can thrive against anyone. When he’s not, like in his brutal performance Sunday, it’s nearly impossible to stop spiraling.</p><p>The Bears were on their way to blowing out the woeful Buccaneers until Williams started throwing interceptions. He veered off track and took the offense with him in a game that was so ugly that Bears coach Ben Johnson said he was “grateful” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/08/bears-buccaneers-inactives-bears-rb-kyle-monangai-remains-out-with-toe-injury" >to win 27-24 on Cairo Santos’ last-second field goal</a>.</p><p>They plunged after taking an early 14-0 lead, and Williams finished with a career-high four interceptions as he completed 22 of 37 passes for 279 yards with two touchdowns for a 61.5 passer rating.</p><p>Williams likely would disagree, but he appeared to get carried away by how unstoppable he had been lately. He carved up the Falcons, Patriots and Seahawks like he was playing a video game and might’ve been overconfident when it came to tight windows, off-balanced throws and general freewheeling.</p><p>“The four interceptions, there are a couple where [he] didn’t see the coverage quite as well as we would’ve liked,” Johnson said Monday. “There’s a couple where we’re making attempts to avoid disaster and we didn’t [burn] it and [live] on for the next play.”</p><p>Johnson also repeatedly credited Bucs coach Todd Bowles and his fourth-ranked defense and said, “There will be [mistakes] for us to put in our memory bank and draw from next time we go against a team like that.”</p><p>Williams opened 11-of-16 passing for 150 yards with two touchdowns for a 138.0 passer rating and had the Bears on the verge of a three-score lead before the interceptions started.</p><p>On second-and-goal from the Bucs’ 21-yard line, Williams threw what he called a “greedy” pass to Rome Odunze in the end zone rather than hit Luther Burden open underneath, and safety Tykee Smith raced in front of Odunze for the interception.</p><p>That began a freefall for Williams and the offense. Williams followed his strong start by completing just 11 of 21 passes for 129 yards and four interceptions, and the Bears’ two dominant drives to start the game faded as they managed two field goals in 12 possessions after that.</p><p>The Bears missed a chance to bury the Bucs by halftime, then went the entire third quarter without picking up a first down. The rushing attack fizzled, too, and running backs D’Andre Swift and Salvon Ahmed combined to average 2.8 yards per carry.</p><p>“We got out of rhythm as an offense,” Johnson said.</p><p>The Bucs pulled within a touchdown early in the fourth quarter and tied it with three minutes left.</p><p>Williams had a rough night, but context is everything. This wasn’t the cause for alarm it would’ve been at any point in his first two seasons.</p><p>Whereas predecessor Justin Fields’ five-turnover game against the Bucs in 2021 fit a pattern, Williams’ dud against them Sunday was an outlier — especially this season.</p><p>Before Sunday, Williams had thrown interceptions on just 1.1% of passes for his career. Aaron Rodgers was at 1.2% in his prime. Williams has earned enough credibility that the occasional poor performance doesn’t raise questions about whether he’s the Bears’ future.</p><p>And, zeroing back in on Sunday itself, he was essential to the winning drive. Williams got tremendous help from his defense, including a pick-six by Jaylon Johnson, but the Bears wouldn’t have won without his 38-yard pass to tight end Colston Loveland with 40 seconds left.</p><p>Teams have to take the good with the bad when young quarterbacks are developing, and Williams has shown promise, but he’s not a finished product yet. By no means does he get a free pass for Sunday, but he’s put forth a lot more good than bad.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Blackhawks' problems start with GM Kyle Davidson
entries.summary: <p>Here’s the thing about rebuilds: They can keep people employed who shouldn’t be.</p><p>We’ve seen it from every team in town. Now we have the Blackhawks, who are in Year 5 of a rebuild that has gone off course.</p><p>After making strides last season and raising expectations this season, the Hawks entered Monday with the second-fewest points in the NHL, nine in 18 games. How bad is that? They’re on pace for 42 points, which would be their fewest in a full season since they totaled 31 in 1953-54, when a full season was 70 games.</p><p>So, yeah, things are bad, and it sure felt like the Hawks hit rock bottom Saturday when the Stanley Cup-champion Hurricanes pummeled them in a 9-2 decision that wasn’t as close as the score indicates. It capped a horrendous 0-3 trip that had observers thinking significant changes could be coming. The team was in crisis, and the coach’s seat appeared to be burning.</p><p>But when the Hawks practiced Monday, the general manager was not present.</p><p>Kyle Davidson began serving as interim GM in October 2021 after Stan Bowman resigned in the wake of the investigation into sexual assault allegations against former video coach Brad Aldrich. The Hawks removed Davidson’s interim tag in March 2022 and have given him carte blanche to rebuild the team as he sees fit.</p><p>“There are some things that we need to fix that are going to take time,” Davidson said then. “Whether it’s three, five years, I don’t have an answer for that now. But we have to do this the right way.”</p><p>Well, three years came and went, and five years are staring at Hawks fans, who are paying a tidy sum to watch bad hockey. So how do eight or 10 years sound? Because at this rate, the team won’t be rebuilt anytime soon, even with star center Connor Bedard around.</p><p>Davidson should’ve addressed all that and more Monday. Instead, he’ll speak to media — and fans — Wednesday. Davidson is in Toronto for GM meetings. His home is on fire, but he’ll put out the blaze in a couple of days. Would a Zoom call have killed him?</p><p>That left coach Jeff Blashill to face the music again. Many thought his job was in peril — it still might be — but there he was, leading practice and blowing the whistle to stop drills that had gone awry.</p><p>“Can’t have it!” he bellowed at one point.</p><p>Blashill, who coached mostly bad Red Wings teams from 2015 to 2022, is in a tough spot again. Like in Detroit, he doesn’t have everything he needs here, but he also isn’t getting enough from what he has. He’s empathetic to the fans’ plight in all of this.</p><p>“I get the disappointment. Our record is what our record is,” he said. “It’s not nearly where the fans thought it would be and not where we want it to be. We’re going to do everything we can to try to grind our way through this, get incrementally better, find our way to wins and, if we can do that, the satisfaction you get is awesome.</p><p>“That’s the only thing I could really say to them. I can promise them whatever I want. That’s pretty much all bull----. We’re trying to grind like crazy to get better results through great process.”</p><p>The process that should be addressed is the one that procures players. Davidson went all in with the teardown, but he hasn’t done the same with the build-up. Yes, he acquired defenseman Bowen Byram and brought back Patrick Kane. But he didn’t do nearly enough to supplement all of his precious prospects with capable veterans. He could’ve addressed that Monday.</p><p>The biggest statement Davidson made in absentia was shipping out backup goalie Arvid Soderblom and calling up Drew Commesso. That’ll get the fans excited for the next home game Thursday, when the boo birds will fly at the first sight of folly. He could’ve tried appealing to fans Monday, too.</p><p>And look who’s coming to town. It’s the Sabres, who went 14 seasons without a playoff berth before earning one last season. How many rebuilds is that? Do you remember the last time the Hawks went 14 seasons without making the playoffs? Of course you don’t, because it hasn’t happened — yet.</p><p>Davidson got lucky getting Connor Bedard with the No. 1 pick in 2023. Did he get unlucky or miscalculate by drafting Artyom Levshunov at No. 2 over Ivan Demidov in 2024? The jury is still out on Anton Frondell, the No. 3 pick in 2025. Meanwhile, other rebuilding teams are passing the Hawks left and right. Davidson could’ve talked about that, too.</p><p>Instead, we wait till Wednesday for Davidson to support the … let’s see … one, two, three … fourth coach he has hired. When the popular perception is that the coach is the problem, it’s not a great look if the person who hired him isn’t there. If Davidson is spread too thin, maybe a director of hockey operations is necessary.</p><p>That way, someone would be there to put out the fire.</p>

entries.title: Bears' Ben Johnson on trade deadline: 'We’ll see if there is another move or two to be made'
entries.summary: <p>While the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> begin to self-scout their team during their bye week, they have one avenue to get better — and a short time to do it.</p><p>The NFL’s trade deadline is 3 p.m. Tuesday. The Bears already made a splash, trading for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons late last month, but have been open to other additions. The Bears could use depth at defensive end and cornerback — and, to a lesser degree, perhaps tackle or tight end. Cornerbacks Riq Woolen and Nahshon Wright — the latter a former Bear — have been connected to Chicago, as has former Bears star Khalil Mack, the Chargers edge rusher.</p><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson said Monday that general manager Ryan Poles and the coaching staff have made the trade deadline part of their regular conversation.</p><p>“I think Ryan is doing a phenomenal job every day,” he said. “He’s going through and seeing how we can improve this roster, what we need the most of. The coordinators are certainly talking every day right now, just with where their concerns lie within the roster. So we’ll see.</p><p>“We’ll see if there is another move or two to be made — or if we stand put. I feel really confident about the guys we have in this locker room right now. And I think we’ve proven at this point that we can find a way to win each and every week with this group.”</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>• Wide receiver Luther Burden was concussed by Rueben Bain Jr. on the hit that forced him to fumble at his own 17 late in the fourth quarter.</p><p>• Rookie receiver Zavion Thomas’ unnecessary roughness penalty at the Bucs’ 8 in the second quarter so bothered Johnson that the coach didn’t play him on offense the rest of the game.</p>

entries.title: Tarik Skubal would liven arms race with Brewers, but Cubs have plenty of pitching needs beyond staff ace
entries.summary: <p>LAS VEGAS — The hot stove is switched on, at least for a little while.</p><p>Baseball’s offseason is underway, though it’s expected to come to a screeching, indefinite halt with an expected lockout at the beginning of next month.</p><p>Until then, though, let the rumors fly.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> arrived at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/08/cubs-gm-meetings-offseason-mlb-lockout-free-agents-trades-rumors-jed-hoyer-pitching-rotation-pitchers" >this week’s GM meetings in Las Vegas</a> in need of pitching, obvious after Jed Hoyer spent his end-of-season press conference hammering home that reworking the staff is Priority No. 1.</p><p>That need is more glaring in the wake of the Brewers’ World Series win, which reframed the Cubs’ task from chasing down their pesky division rivals to chasing down the kings of the baseball world.</p><p>“They’ve had the best record in baseball the last two years,” Hoyer said of the Brewers last month. “Both having them in our division having the best record in baseball and being in the National League, the standard has to be exceptionally high.</p><p>“Their pitching has been exceptionally good. That’s the area that we have to double down and really focus on.”</p><p>Jacob Misiorowski blazes fastballs past batters, and the Brewers’ bullpen is replete with weapons no batter wants to face, having just dazzled with a 1.38 ERA in 65 playoff innings.</p><p>The Cubs, meanwhile, after finishing 14 games back in the NL Central standings, have nothing but question marks when it comes to figuring out what their staff will look like when the 2027 season begins.</p><p>All five pitchers who finished the season in the starting rotation are free agents, the in-house candidates to replace them are coming off significant injuries, and the bullpen is likely due for a makeover after Hoyer bluntly critiqued his own work in putting together the 2026 relief corps.</p><p>That’s a lot.</p><p>The shiny bauble out there for Cubs fans to dream about suiting up in blue pinstripes is Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young winner who headlines this offseason’s otherwise lackluster free-agent class.</p><p>He’s sure to get a massive payday, and while the Cubs have been reported both as likely to jump into the bidding war and unlikely to even sniff it, Skubal is exactly the sort of prize that would liven up an intra-division arms race and get the Cubs closer to the champs.</p><p>The best way to match a Misiorowski? How about a Skubal?</p><p>The Dodgers tried that, of course, to no success. Skubal was their big trade-deadline import as they sought a three-peat. The Brewers swept them out of the NLCS.</p><p>Unlike the Dodgers — and much to their fans’ frustrations — the Cubs haven’t made spending big free-agent bucks a habit, even though last winter’s $175 million deal for Alex Bregman dented the narrative a tad. Bregman showed exactly what paying for high-end talent gets you, playing Gold Glove defense and finishing the season as the lineup’s second best hitter after a sluggish start to his Cubs career.</p><p>But Skubal’s contract figures to be in another stratosphere, dollar-wise, and with the Cubs needing so much more than just one arm to improve their pitching, he could very well be beyond what they’re willing to pay.</p><p>After Cubs pitchers gave up more homers than almost every other team in baseball last season, Hoyer talked of the need to nab groundball and strikeout types to complement the Cubs’ elite defense. That’s what he tried to do with deadline acquisitions Clay Holmes and Kevin Gausman, though that didn’t equal the lengthy playoff run he hoped, the Cubs out of the playoffs after just two games.</p><p>A Holmes reunion would make sense, possibly coming at a price that would allow Hoyer to keep adding impact arms, something dropping big money on Skubal could potentially preclude.</p><p>Regardless, the Cubs have made no bones about what the expectation is at Clark and Addison: to play championship-caliber baseball. Their small-market neighbors to the north did just that this year.</p><p>“I watched the World Series,” Bregman said after winning a Gold Glove last month. “We wanted to be playing in that last game and winning that last game.”</p><p>Is there any suite of pitching moves that can get the Cubs to the Brewers’ level? Would betting big on Skubal be the best way to close the gap?</p><p>That’s what Hoyer & Co. have to figure out this winter.</p>

entries.title: Class of 2027 Illinois congressional delegation arrives in Washington
entries.summary: <p>Newly elected members of the Illinois congressional delegation on Sunday began a two-week “freshman” orientation in Washington — just days after Democrats swept races across the country in a repudiation of Trump administration policies.</p><p>The state will see five new faces in Congress next year after a series of retirements created a seismic shift in Illinois politics. Senator-elect Juliana Stratton arrived in Washington on Monday for a two-day Senate orientation after winning the open race to succeed Sen. Dick Durbin.</p><p>And yes, there is a group chat for the five incoming members of the House: Daniel Biss, Patty Garcia, Melissa Bean, Donna Morgan and La Shawn Ford. Bean, who won the 8th Congressional District after Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi opted to run for the Senate seat, is not a new face in Congress. She previously represented the district from 2005 to 2011.</p><p>“We're connecting throughout the day," Garcia said.</p><p>"Some of us came in earlier. Daniel Biss and myself came in earlier for the Congressional Progressive Caucus. Some of the other members came in earlier for the New Dems caucus,” she added. “It was a day focused more on, what is the progressive agenda for us? What are we fighting for? What are making sure that is front and center as we work with other Dems and leadership?"</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure A post-lunch session was called “If I knew then what I know now” with fellow members of Congress.</p><p>House Leader Hakeem Jeffries is holding an event Tuesday nigh for Democratic members-elect and their spouses at the U.S. Capitol’s Statuary Hall. There’s also a reception for members at the Library of Congress Wednesday evening and a Saturday night reception at the National Air and Space Museum.</p><p>Garcia said the newly elected Illinois Democrats are sharing ideas about what they want to accomplish next year.</p><p>“I know for me, having been working on the immigration front and knowing how critical it is to ensure that we have allies on immigration, I know that I'm going take it upon my upon myself to coordinate the new members to do an immigration briefing with some of our trusted immigration organizations and lawyers that can walk us through the big picture,” Garcia said. “Here's immigration policy, and then here's some of the recent kinds of initiatives and moving forward, what we need to do as a Democratic caucus.”</p><p>Beyond orientation, members are also trying to secure coveted committee assignments. New members typically submit their list of preferred committees to a steering and outreach committee.</p><p>Garcia is aiming for the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the influential House Judiciary Committee. But I think that being in a position to have the House and the Senate is a great deterrent for corruption for the president. I mean, that's why we have to have strong leadership in Congress — so that we could do both.”</p>

entries.title: City sports commission hopes better terms can be met for hosting 2031 Women's World Cup
entries.summary: <p>Whether Chicago wins the race to host the 2031 Women’s World Cup games could come down to agreeable terms for the city’s venues, according to the head of the Chicago Sports Commission.</p><p>Chicago is among more than two dozen cities in the Western Hemisphere with their eyes already set on a shot at hosting matches in 2031. A delegation of FIFA officials will vote on the host countries for the tournament Nov. 23.</p><p>No binding documents have been signed, said commission executive director Kara Bachman, though she said Soldier Field is the city's top pick to host in its application.</p><p>But if Chicago were selected, it would be the city's first World Cup matches since 1999, when it hosted a sold-out crowd of more than 65,000 at Soldier Field for a group-stage match between the U.S. Women’s National Team and Nigeria. Chicago has dropped two bids to host games since then.</p><h3>Better terms, better chances</h3><p>Bachman said the city likely would make Soldier Field the “primary venue,” and that "other venues are being explored," but wouldn’t give specifics about if that included venues like SeatGeek Stadium in Bridgeview or McDonald's Park, the Chicago Fire stadium under being built at The 78.</p><p>“We won’t know about game allocation until further down the road,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a The stadium could be one of the venues included in Chicago’s bid for the 2031 Women’s World Cup.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>For now, one of the city’s main considerations is how hosting the Women’s World Cup could impact Soldier Field’s schedule.</p><p>Bachman said a main issue for the city is exclusivity clauses. According to FIFA, the soccer organization requires venues to shut down for a set number of days before and after the games for necessary setup and tear-down.</p><p>Soldier Field's schedule is often packed with concerts and other sporting events through the summer when the tournament would potentially take place. City officials haven't historically been willing to give those events up for tournaments.</p><p>Contract clauses also played a role in 2018, when then-Mayor Rahm Emmanuel <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/3/14/18447724/emanuel-pulls-chicago-out-of-world-cup-bid" target="_blank" ><u>had Chicago drop its bid</u></a> to host the 2026 men’s tournament due to “uncertainty for taxpayers," such as the city being <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/3/15/18439811/emanuel-aide-chicago-balked-at-blank-check-demand-for-world-cup" >on the hook to cover unlimited cost overruns</a>.</p><p>“Ultimately we concluded that while the opportunity to be a World Cup city was very attractive, it wasn't going to work for the terms [in 2018],” Bachman said.</p><p>This time, the exclusive use period for tournament venues in 2031 would be 14 days before the first match at the venue and five days after the last match ended, according to a FIFA spokesperson. That means if Chicago were selected for even a single match, the exclusivity clause would lock Soldier Field down for a minimum of 20 days. </p><p>Apply that to the 2027 Women's World Cup, which Brazil alone is hosting. The country's Arena de Pernambuco will see seven games over 13 days, the shortest span among the eight stadiums in use there. Under the 2031 terms, that would put the stadium in FIFA's hands for just over a month.</p><p>Bachman said that's still an improvement over the terms the city was offered in 2018 for the 2026 men's games: 30 days prior to the first game and seven days after the last.</p><p> “This seems less invasive compared to the [2026] men's World Cup request," Bachman said.</p><div class="Enhancement" C. plays Crystal Palace in the Chicago Nations Cup at SeatGeek on July 26, 2023.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Michael Reaves/Getty</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Midwest in the running</h3><p>FIFA likely won't make a decision on potential host cities for a few years, Bachman said. FIFA declined to confirm a timeline.</p><p>But there are strong contenders for the tournament across the Midwest. Among Chicago's regional rivals are Kansas City, Missouri, Cleveland, Columbus, Minneapolis, Detroit and Indianapolis.</p><p>Soldier Field, Detroit’s Ford Field, Cleveland’s Huntington Bank Field and Kansas City’s Arrowhead Stadium all hold roughly 62,000 to 69,000 spectators. Minneapolis’ U.S. Bank Stadium and Indianapolis’ Lucas Oil Stadium have both been expanded beyond 70,000 seats for special events. And </p><p>Kansas City stands as one of Chicago’s toughest competitors in the bid for games thanks to its facilities. It has recent World Cup experience, having hosted several games in the 2026 men’s tournament. The Kansas City Current's two-year-old CPKC Stadium was the first built expressly for women's soccer when it opened for the 2024 season. And Arrowhead is being replaced in 2031 with a 70,000 seat domed stadium.</p><p>Still, with the Fire breaking its seasonal attendance record for the fourth year in a row and the Red Stars holding the NWSL's single-game attendance record, Bachman feels the landscape — especially for women's sports — could make the timing right.</p><p>“For Chicago, being as diverse a city as we are that has all the major sports, we would be a tremendous host," Bachman said. "I think there's a great opportunity to work with other U.S cities to put our country on display in a positive way."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/16/chicago-puts-in-bid-to-host-fifa-2031-womens-world-cup" >Chicago puts in bid to host 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/3/14/18447724/emanuel-pulls-chicago-out-of-world-cup-bid" >Emanuel pulls Chicago out of World Cup bid</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
